paras: The death of Fred Spencer near Mulga, Alabama, came to light in early August 1910, when the body of a Black man believed to be Spencer was found there. Spencer had been sought since April as the accused killer of Capt. B. H. Young, and a Birmingham paper wrote that it was "possible that he was lynched" by men who had hunted him.

According to the Birmingham Age-Herald's Bessemer column, Spencer was "the slayer of Capt. B. H. Young in April"; no report of the killing itself or of any charge appears in the coverage. The column recalled that "Bessemer was stirred up at the time of the killing" and that "posses of men" from the town searched the woods for him. Members of those posses declared that if Spencer were found he "would never reach the county jail alive."

On or about August 1, residents of Bessemer learned that the body of a Black man had been found near Mulga and that it was believed to be Spencer's. The item did not describe the condition of the body, how the man died, or who identified him. Pointing to the posse members' earlier threat, the correspondent suggested that Spencer might have been lynched.
No report of an inquest, a confirmed identification, or any arrest appears in the coverage.

The only report found ran on August 2, 1910, in the Birmingham Age-Herald, as a short paragraph headed "Interest in Discovery of Body" within its Bessemer news column. Placed among notices of club meetings, a wedding and a Confederate veterans' gathering, the item called Spencer "the slayer" without qualification and reported the posse's vow and the possible lynching without comment. The same column remarked on the scarcity of Black prisoners for the Bessemer street gang that week.
No coverage of the case in the Black press, or in other white papers, was found.
